newsitem.title: UK: British parties level on economy - Reuters/NOP poll.
newsitem.headline: British parties level on economy - Reuters/NOP poll.

text.p: Britain's voters see little to choose between Labour and Conservative parties when it comes to managing the economy, an exclusive Reuters poll showed on Tuesday.
The survey, conducted by leading polling organisation NOP, found that the ruling Conservative and main opposition Labour parties were running neck-and-neck over economic issues.

Asked which party could be best trusted to manage the economy, 32 percent backed the Conservatives and 30 percent Labour, despite the government's chequered economic record and the host of tax rises it has levied since 1992.

NOP polled 1,049 people across 51 parliamentary constituencies last Friday. Despite the close call on economic issues, the survey gave Labour a 20-point lead overall. A general election must be held by May 22 and is widely tipped to take place on May 1.

The poll, which focused closely on the top economic issues likely to dominate the election, suggests the Conservatives may start to reap the benefits of an economic upturn which is now entering its fifth consecutive year.

While male voters backed Labour narrowly by 33 percent to 32 percent on this issue, female voters remained wary of Labour with just 28 percent trusting Labour most with the economy against 32 percent for the Conservatives.
Voters remained suspicious of Labour, which has remodelled its economic policies and spruced up its image, on the two top levers of economic management -- interest rates and taxes.

A quarter of voters in the survey felt mortgage rates (crucial in Britain where two thirds of households borrow to buy their own homes) would be higher under a Labour government, while 16 percent felt mortgage rates would be higher under the Conservatives.

Concern over Labour and mortgage rates was most marked in the 35-54 age group, with 30 percent seeing rates higher under Labour against 15 percent viewing the Conservative party as the harbinger of higher mortgage costs.

Asked about the total taxes people have to pay -- including value added tax and council tax -- 32 percent of respondents felt taxes would be higher under a Labour government against 19 percent who felt Conservative governments mean higher taxes.

The Conservative lead on the tax issue was most marked in the AB professional class group, with a lead of 47 percent to 11 percent, but continued into the key C2 skilled manual worker group at 28 percent to 21 percent.
Labour has been trying to shed its reputation as a tax-and-spend party and has pledged not to raise the main income tax rates during the next parliament if it wins the election.

The poll found far more voters feel the economy is now doing well or fairly well as opposed to badly -- holding out hope for Prime Minister John Major that he may yet reap the benefits of economic success, the so-called "feelgood" factor.

More than half those surveyed, 51 percent, said the economy was doing either fairly well (42 percent) or very well (nine percent), against 21 percent who said it was doing fairly badly and 10 percent who labelled economic performance very bad.
Of those who said the economy was doing fairly well, 27 percent said the government was mainly reponsible, with 22 percent crediting company managers and 15 percent efforts by British workers.
